title: Hemodynamic Effects of Anesthetics, Sedatives, and Analgesics in the CICU: JACC State-of-the-Art Review
category: Hemodynamic Effects of Anesthetics, Sedatives, and Analgesics in the CICU
excerpt: Original source: Safiullah, Z, Applefeld, W, Li, W. et al. Hemodynamic Effects of Anesthetics, Sedatives, and Analgesics in the CICU: Clinical Decision Guidance. JACC Adv. 2026 Aug, 5 (8). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.103017
body:
Pharmacokinetic properties of drugs such as metabolism and elimination can be altered in the setting of end-organ dysfunction, particularly in shock states characterized by multisystem dysfunction, presenting an additional challenge in caring for critically ill patients.

Many agents used to maintain amnesia, comfort, and safety for the patient can negatively impact hemodynamic parameters and respiratory status, making careful selection vital to optimize overall stability.

Anesthetics induce a reversible anterograde amnesia, analgesia, and muscle relaxation, often necessitating ventilatory and hemodynamic support.

Sedatives can have effects ranging from conscious sedation to coma by decreasing the level of consciousness in a dose-dependent fashion, with deeper levels frequently impairing respiratory drive and cardiovascular function.

Analgesics decrease the perception of pain or discomfort and can produce states of euphoria; however, doses that are adequate to produce elimination of any pain perception typically also carry the risk of respiratory depression and hypotension.

HEMODYNAMICS OF SHOCK STATES

Cardiogenic shock (CS)

  • Ineffective CO leads to critical end-organ hypoperfusion.

  • Prevalence of 65% in cardiovascular intensive care unit (CICU) shock patients.

  • Mortality rate of 40% to 50%

  • Nuanced understanding of preload and afterload is critical to support myocardial function without imposing an excessive oxygen demand or aggravating ventricular workload.

  • Advanced monitoring modalities and diagnostic tools (eg, pulmonary artery catheterization, intra-arterial lines, and echocardiography) are often essential to guide hemodynamic support prior to and during the administration of anesthetics, sedatives, and analgesics.

Vasodilatory shock

  • prevalence of 12% among all CICU patients presenting with shock

  • The sepsis cohort of CICU patients tend to be older with more chronic comorbidity and have fewer acute organ failures than their counterparts in noncardiac ICUs, albeit with a similar rate of mortality

  • ↓SVR, ↑CO (likely due to decreased afterload, increased sympathetic drive and stress response, exogenous catecholamines, and cardiac compensation)

Mixed shock

  • can be defined as primary, cardiogenic-vasodilatory, or vasodilatory-cardiogenic.

  • prevalence of 20% in the modern CICU.

  • ↓SVR (common in mixed shock; can be caused by sterile vasoplegia or sepsis).

  • Mixed shock states have a similar in-hospital mortality rate to CS (23%-55%).

Cardiogenic shock with RV failure

prevalence of 25% to 60% of patients with acute pulmonary embolism and 7% of patients with AMI-CS.

associated with increased mortality compared to isolated LV failure.

↑RV afterload and RV-pulmonary artery uncoupling → reduced RV stroke volume → RV dilation → leftward interventricular septal displacement → limiting left heart filling → ↓CO and ↓MAP → ↓ right heart coronary perfusion pressure → ↓RV oxygen supply → worsening ischemia to the right heart ("RV death spiral").

Management strategies include optimizing preload, reducing RV afterload, enhancing inotropy, and maintaining RV perfusion.

ENDOTRACHEAL INTUBATION IN CRITICALLY ILL CARDIAC PATIENTS

Endotracheal intubation (ETI) of critically ill patients is associated with peri-intubation complications, such as hemodynamic instability and cardiac arrest, with prevalence of 42.6% and 3.1%, respectively.
